stage_a.note: Delivery is engaged and professional with clear positive moments, though largely matter-of-fact.
Engaged animation recurs at meaningful points but alternates with subdued delivery.
Professional and approachable orientation apparent at several points alongside impersonal stretches.

venture.description: Sweat-activated apparel technology that reveals hidden messages or logos when the fabric gets wet.
venture.note: The founder is currently selling shirts but ultimately wants to license the technology to major apparel brands.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben introduces ViewSport, a sweat-activated technology built into t-shirts that reveals a hidden logo when the wearer sweats.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Kevin asks what the sales are for the company.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben states they have done $140,000 in sales this year, with 80% coming in the last three months.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert asks if he can see one of the shirts.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben hands out sample shirts to the investors to examine.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Mark asks if Ben invented the technology himself or if he licensed it.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben confirms it is his technology, he invented it, and it is currently patent pending.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert asks how Ben invented the technology.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben explains his background in chemistry and how he noticed sweat patterns while working out during medical school.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert asks if Ben quit medical school to pursue this full-time.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben confirms he dropped out of medical school and is doing this full-time.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert expresses skepticism about whether the technology would actually motivate a consumer to buy the shirt.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben clarifies that it is not just about the shirt, but the technology acting as a new medium for branding.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Kevin asks if the strategy is to license the technology to players in the apparel business.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben confirms that licensing to apparel players and integrating into other textiles is the strategy.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert asks if the $140,000 in sales came from licensing.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben explains that the sales are from full decoration services, applying the chemical to other people's shirts.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Barbara asks if the user has to sweat to see the imprint.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben confirms that sweating is required, noting it as the beauty of the technology, and mentions kids in water parks.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Barbara challenges the utility, noting that the user has to be wet to see the message.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben acknowledges that the user does have to be wet for the logo to appear.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert asks if the model would work if Ben simply provided the chemical or the way to make it.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben agrees, stating that licensing out the technology is the ultimate end game.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert asks if Ben has approached any companies about a licensing deal.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben says they have approached companies and mentions that Hurley is currently very interested.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Barbara asks how hard someone has to work out to sweat enough to reveal the logo.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben replies that a 20-minute workout for an average individual will produce the results.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert points out that the logo goes away pretty quickly.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben explains that sweating from the inside works better than spraying water from the outside.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Mark sprays a shirt to test it, and the investors banter as the logo fails to appear clearly.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Mark asks if Ben has had any complaints from customers about the logo not being visible.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben denies having any complaints and states that the visibility issue never happens in practice.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Barbara examines a shirt and points out that the material seems to be falling apart.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben shows another sample shirt to the panel to demonstrate the effect more clearly.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Kevin asks if the technology can be applied to 100% cotton material.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben confirms that while the current shirt is polyester, it can be done on 100% cotton.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Barbara asks if the secondary word can be in a contrasting color like black to make it pop.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben explains that it is currently all monochromatic, but he is working on adding colors.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Daymond asks what Ben plans to use the half a million dollars for.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben says the money will be used to drive awareness and get the technology into major brands.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Daymond challenges that the investors are paying now for a brand awareness that doesn't exist yet.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Daymond asks if Ben sees a problem with asking them to pay for future, unproven awareness.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben defends the valuation by projecting half a million in sales by the end of the year.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Daymond points out that if he hits those projections, he wouldn't need their money.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben responds that while he might not need the money, he needs their relationships.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Daymond argues that this means he would be working for his own money.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben emphasizes that the technology has inherent value that the investors should recognize.

turns.speaker: S5
turns.summary: Daymond decides to exit, feeling the valuation is too high for what is currently established.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben volunteers that they just received a purchase order from the US Naval Academy for 1500 shirts.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Kevin asks Ben to reverse engineer the valuation to justify asking for a $2.5 million value.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben states that the investor should be making $500,000 to justify the valuation.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Kevin asks how much Ben is currently making.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben reiterates that they have made $140,000 so far.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Kevin challenges the valuation, stating Ben is making squat while charging a massive multiple.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben argues he is looking for a partnership to help the business grow based on the great technology.

turns.speaker: S3
turns.summary: Mark exits, stating Ben strategized incorrectly by asking for too much money when he really needs their help.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Kevin asks why he would give money at a valuation that guarantees he will never get a return.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben tries to justify the valuation by pointing out that the apparel industry is a $54 billion market.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Kevin dismisses the market size argument, saying every entrepreneur uses that line.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben notes that even Nike only has a 4% market share because the market is highly fragmented.

turns.speaker: S1
turns.summary: Kevin exits, feeling financially insulted by the arrogant valuation and the strategic mistake.

turns.speaker: S4
turns.summary: Barbara exits, stating the product is terrible, too monochromatic, and requires too much sweat.

turns.speaker: S2
turns.summary: Robert exits, saying he is not sold on the product and thinks it is a bit gimmicky.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.summary: Ben thanks the investors for their time.

exchanges.label: testing the shirt with water spray

decisions.note: believes founder wants money without giving up enough value
founder strategized incorrectly and asked for too much money
feels financially insulted by the high valuation and arrogance
finds the product terrible, too monochromatic, and requires too much sweat
not sold on the product, thinks it is a bit gimmicky

record.notes: The pitch features a model, Cody, who demonstrates the shirt but does not speak or participate in the discussion, so he is not listed as an actor.
